## Welcome {#home}

### Basic Biostatistics

**Learning Objectives:**

- Distinguish qualitative from quantitative data and choose an
  appropriate presentation method
- Calculate and interpret the mean, median, and mode
- Calculate and interpret the range, standard deviation, and
  coefficient of variation
- Describe the properties of the normal distribution
- Distinguish probability from non-probability sampling techniques
- Apply the t-test and chi-square test to appropriate data types
- Distinguish correlation from regression

**NMC Community Medicine Code:** CM6

🟢 **MUST KNOW** · 🟡 **SHOULD KNOW** · 🟣 **MAY KNOW** · 🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.notes}
This chapter gives the statistical toolkit that Chapter 3's rates and
ratios, Chapter 4's study designs, and Chapter 5's screening validity
measures all quietly assume — the numbers behind the numbers. It closes
the curriculum as its own standalone subject area, since NMC's CBME
blueprint treats basic biostatistics as a distinct competency domain
from epidemiology itself.
:::

## Types of Data {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Choosing the right statistical technique starts with knowing what kind
of data you have:

- **Qualitative (categorical) data** — describes a quality/attribute,
  not a quantity
  - **Nominal** — unordered categories (blood group, sex, religion)
  - **Ordinal** — ordered categories without equal intervals (mild/
    moderate/severe; socioeconomic class)
- **Quantitative (numerical) data** — measured on a numeric scale
  - **Discrete** — whole-number counts only (number of children, number
    of episodes of diarrhoea)
  - **Continuous** — any value within a range (height, blood pressure,
    haemoglobin level)

**Why this distinction matters first:** it determines everything that
follows — which measure of central tendency is meaningful, which chart
type applies, and which test of significance is valid for that data
type.

---

## Presenting Data {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

Raw data must be organized before it can be interpreted — the same
"choosing the right format" logic already introduced for population
health data (Chapter 21), applied here to any dataset:

- **Tables** — precise values, ordered rows/columns, the basis for
  every other presentation format
- **Bar diagram** — compares categories (qualitative or discrete data);
  bar height/length represents frequency
- **Pie chart** — shows proportions of a whole
- **Histogram** — for continuous data grouped into class intervals;
  unlike a bar diagram, bars touch since the underlying scale is
  continuous
- **Line diagram** — shows a trend over time (e.g. monthly disease
  incidence)
- **Statistical (spot) map** — shows geographic distribution of a
  variable across areas/regions (e.g. district-wise disease incidence
  shaded on a map) — the same logic John Snow applied by hand-plotting
  cholera deaths around the Broad Street pump (Chapter 3)

**Exam tip:** a histogram's bars touch; a bar diagram's bars don't —
this single visual distinction encodes the deeper point that histograms
represent a continuous scale with no natural gaps between categories.

---

## Measures of Central Tendency {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Three ways to describe a "typical" value in a dataset, each suited to
different circumstances:

- **Mean** — the arithmetic average (sum of values ÷ number of values);
  uses every value, but is **pulled toward outliers/skewed data**
- **Median** — the middle value when data is arranged in order; **not
  affected by extreme outliers**, making it the better choice for
  skewed distributions (e.g. income, hospital length of stay)
- **Mode** — the most frequently occurring value; the only measure of
  central tendency usable for **nominal (categorical) data**

**Choosing between them:** symmetric, non-skewed continuous data → mean;
skewed continuous data or data with outliers → median; categorical data
→ mode.

---

## Measures of Dispersion {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Central tendency alone can be misleading — two datasets can share the
same mean while looking very different in spread:

- **Range** — highest value minus lowest value; simplest measure, but
  entirely determined by the two most extreme values
- **Standard deviation (SD)** — the average distance of each value from
  the mean; the most widely used measure of spread for data that is
  roughly normally distributed
- **Variance** — the square of the SD; used mathematically (e.g. in
  further statistical tests) more often than reported directly
- **Coefficient of variation (CV)** — SD expressed as a percentage of
  the mean (`CV = (SD / Mean) × 100`); allows comparing the relative
  spread of two datasets measured in **different units** (e.g. comparing
  variability in height vs. weight)

**Why CV matters specifically:** SD alone can't compare variability
across different scales — a SD of 5 kg and a SD of 5 cm aren't
comparable, but their CVs are.

---

## The Normal Distribution {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

Many biological measurements (height, blood pressure, haemoglobin)
approximate a **normal (Gaussian) distribution** — a symmetric,
bell-shaped curve with defining properties:

- **Mean = median = mode**, all at the centre of the curve
- Symmetric about the mean — the two tails mirror each other
- **68–95–99.7 rule:** approximately 68% of values fall within ±1 SD of
  the mean, 95% within ±2 SD, and 99.7% within ±3 SD

**Why this matters practically:** it's what makes the SD interpretable
— knowing the mean and SD of a normally distributed variable tells you,
without seeing the raw data, roughly what range most values fall in,
and what counts as an unusually extreme value.

---

## Sampling Techniques {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

Studying an entire population is rarely feasible — a **sample** is
selected to represent it, using one of two broad approaches:

- **Probability sampling** (every unit has a known, non-zero chance of
  selection — allows valid generalization to the population):
  - **Simple random sampling** — every unit has an equal chance,
    selected via random numbers
  - **Systematic sampling** — every *k*th unit selected from a list
  - **Stratified sampling** — population divided into homogeneous
    strata (e.g. by age group) first, then randomly sampled within each
  - **Cluster sampling** — naturally occurring groups (e.g. villages,
    schools) are randomly selected, and every unit within a chosen
    cluster is included
- **Non-probability sampling** (selection not random — convenient but
  cannot support valid generalization): convenience, purposive, and
  quota sampling

**Why the distinction matters:** only probability sampling provides a
statistical basis for generalizing findings from the sample back to
the population — the entire logic of inferential statistics that
follows depends on it.

---

## Sample Size {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

An appropriately calculated sample size balances two competing risks:
too small a sample risks missing a real effect (inadequate statistical
power); too large wastes time, cost, and participant burden without
added benefit.

**Key factors that increase the required sample size:**

- Higher desired **confidence level** (e.g. 99% vs. 95%)
- Smaller **expected effect size** (a subtle difference needs more
  participants to detect reliably than an obvious one)
- Greater **variability** in the outcome being measured
- Higher desired **statistical power** (the ability to detect a true
  effect if one exists)

**Why this belongs in a curriculum, not just a statistics course:** an
underpowered study (Chapter 4) can fail to detect a real association
purely because it enrolled too few participants — not because no
association exists.

---

## Standard Error and Confidence Intervals {background-color="#E3F2E1"}

🟢 **MUST KNOW**

- **Standard Error (SE)** — the standard deviation of the *sample mean*
  itself, estimating how much a sample mean would vary if the study
  were repeated; `SE = SD / √n` — **SE shrinks as sample size grows**,
  unlike SD, which describes spread within a single sample and doesn't
  shrink with larger n
- **Confidence interval (CI)** — a range, calculated from the sample
  mean ± a multiple of the SE, that is expected to contain the true
  population value with a stated level of confidence (typically 95%)

**Why SE matters for tests of significance:** every test on the
following slides ultimately compares an observed difference to the
amount of variation expected by chance alone — and that expected
variation is expressed using the standard error.

---

## Tests of Significance: The t-test {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

The **t-test** compares the **means** of continuous data between two
groups (or a sample mean against a known value), asking: is the
observed difference larger than what chance alone would produce?

- **Unpaired (independent) t-test** — compares means between two
  separate, independent groups (e.g. mean blood pressure in a treated
  vs. untreated group)
- **Paired t-test** — compares means from the **same** subjects measured
  twice (e.g. before and after an intervention), accounting for the
  natural correlation between paired measurements

**p-value:** the probability of observing a difference this large (or
larger) if there were truly no difference in the population; by
convention, **p < 0.05** is considered statistically significant — but
statistical significance is not the same as clinical importance.

---

## Tests of Significance: Chi-Square Test {background-color="#FFF6DA"}

🟡 **SHOULD KNOW**

The **chi-square (χ²) test** is used for **categorical data**, testing
whether the observed distribution across categories differs from what
would be expected by chance — e.g. is disease frequency associated with
exposure status, when both are categorical (present/absent)?

`χ² = Σ [(Observed − Expected)² / Expected]`

**Why it's the categorical counterpart to the t-test:** the t-test
needs continuous data with means to compare; chi-square instead compares
**counts/frequencies** across categories — the correct tool once data
is nominal or ordinal rather than a measurable numeric scale.

---

## Correlation and Regression {background-color="#E8E4F3"}

🟣 **MAY KNOW**

- **Correlation** — measures the **strength and direction** of a linear
  relationship between two continuous variables, expressed as the
  correlation coefficient (*r*, ranging from −1 to +1); *r* close to 0
  means little or no linear relationship
- **Regression** — goes further than correlation by modelling how one
  variable **predicts or changes with** another, producing an equation
  that can estimate one variable's value from the other

**Exam tip, revisited from Chapter 4:** correlation and regression both
describe association, not causation — the same causal-inference caution
already introduced in the Bradford Hill criteria (Chapter 2) applies
directly here.

## Self-Check: Question 1 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 1

A dataset of hospital length-of-stay (in days) contains a few very
long outlier admissions. Which measure of central tendency best
represents the "typical" stay?

- Mean
- [Median]{.correct data-explanation="The median is not affected by extreme outliers, making it the better choice for skewed data like length-of-stay, where a few very long admissions would pull the mean upward."}
- Mode
- Range
:::

## Self-Check: Question 2 {background-color="#FDE8E8"}

🧡 **QUESTION**

::: {.quiz-question}
### Question 2

Under the 68-95-99.7 rule for a normally distributed variable,
approximately what proportion of values fall within ±2 standard
deviations of the mean?

- 68%
- [95%]{.correct data-explanation="Approximately 95% of values in a normal distribution fall within plus-or-minus 2 standard deviations of the mean, with 99.7% falling within plus-or-minus 3 SD."}
- 99.7%
- 50%
:::

### Question 4

Comparing mean fasting blood glucose in the same patients before and
after a 12-week diet intervention calls for which test?

- Unpaired t-test
- [Paired t-test]{.correct data-explanation="A paired t-test is used when the same subjects are measured twice (before and after), since it accounts for the natural correlation between each person's two measurements."}
- Chi-square test
- Correlation coefficient
:::
